title: Kubernetes
blurb: Orchestrating containers at scale -- pods, Deployments, Services, Ingress, and autoscaling.

lessons.title: Why container orchestration exists
objectives: Explain the problem Kubernetes solves beyond what Docker alone provides
Explain how container orchestration changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect container orchestration with desired state and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Docker packages and runs a single container well, but production systems need many containers across many machines, restarted automatically when they crash, scaled up under load, and rolled out without downtime.
examples:
# Docker alone: you manually run/restart containers on one machine
# Kubernetes: you declare 'I want 3 replicas of this container running'
# and the cluster continuously enforces that, across many machines,
# restarting failed ones and rescheduling if a machine goes down
commonMistakes: Assuming Docker alone is sufficient for production -- Docker runs containers; Kubernetes is what keeps many containers running correctly, at scale, across failures, without manual.
lessons.careerRelevance: Nearly every backend role at a company running containers at scale expects familiarity with Kubernetes, not just Docker.

lessons.title: Kubernetes architecture: control plane & nodes
objectives: Describe the roles of the control plane and worker nodes
Explain how control plane changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect control plane with API server and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A Kubernetes cluster has a control plane (the brain: the API server, which everything talks to; the scheduler, which decides where new workloads run; and etcd, which stores the cluster's actual state) and worker nodes (machines that actually run your containers, each running a kubelet agent that talks to the control plane).
examples:
# conceptual flow:
# kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
# -> API server receives the desired state
# -> scheduler decides which node(s) should run it
# -> kubelet on that node actually starts the container
commonMistakes: Trying to manage containers by directly SSHing into nodes -- this bypasses Kubernetes entirely and the control plane will fight you, since it continuously tries to reconcile actual state.
lessons.careerRelevance: Understanding this architecture is assumed baseline knowledge in any Kubernetes-related interview question.

lessons.title: kubectl: the primary interface to a cluster
objectives: Use kubectl to inspect and manage basic cluster resources
Explain how kubectl get changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect kubectl get with kubectl describe and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: kubectl is the command-line tool for talking to a cluster's API server -- nearly everything you do with Kubernetes goes through it. kubectl get lists resources, kubectl describe shows detailed info (including recent events, invaluable for debugging), kubectl apply -f applies a YAML file's desired state, and kubectl logs shows a container's output.
examples:
kubectl get pods
kubectl describe pod my-app-7d4f9
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl logs my-app-7d4f9
commonMistakes: Jumping straight to kubectl logs when a pod won't start -- kubectl describe usually surfaces the actual problem (like a failed image pull or resource limit) in its Events section, before.
lessons.careerRelevance: kubectl fluency is a practical, daily-use skill expected in any role touching a real Kubernetes cluster.

lessons.title: Deployments & ReplicaSets
objectives: Explain how a Deployment manages replicas and enables safe rollouts
Explain how Deployment changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Deployment with ReplicaSet and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: You rarely create bare pods directly in production -- a Deployment manages a ReplicaSet, which ensures a specified number of identical pod replicas are running at all times, automatically replacing any that crash or get deleted.
examples:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-app
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: my-app:2.0
commonMistakes: Manually creating and managing individual pods instead of a Deployment -- you lose automatic replacement on crash, easy scaling, and safe rolling updates, all of which a Deployment gives you.
lessons.careerRelevance: Deployments are the single most commonly used Kubernetes object in real production workloads.
lessons.explain: You rarely create bare pods directly in production -- a Deployment manages a ReplicaSet, which ensures a specified number of identical pod replicas are running at all times, automatically replacing any that crash or get deleted.

lessons.title: Services: stable networking for pods
objectives: Explain why Services exist and the main Service types
Explain how Service changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Service with ClusterIP and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Pods are ephemeral -- they get replaced constantly, and each replacement gets a new IP address. A Service provides a single, stable IP address and DNS name that automatically routes traffic to whichever healthy pods currently match its label selector, so other parts of your system never need to track individual pod IPs directly.
examples:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-app-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: my-app
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 8080
commonMistakes: Hardcoding a pod's IP address anywhere in application config -- pod IPs change constantly as pods are replaced; always target a Service's stable address instead.
lessons.careerRelevance: Services are how literally everything in a real Kubernetes cluster actually talks to everything else.
lessons.explain: Pods are ephemeral -- they get replaced constantly, and each replacement gets a new IP address. lessons.title: ConfigMaps & Secrets
objectives: Externalize configuration and sensitive data from container images
Explain how ConfigMap changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect ConfigMap with Secret and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A ConfigMap holds non-sensitive configuration (URLs, feature flags, config files) as key-value data that can be injected into pods as environment variables or mounted files -- keeping config separate from the container image so the same image works across environments.
examples:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata: {name: app-config}
data:
  API_URL: "https://api.example.com"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata: {name: app-secret}
data:
  DB_PASSWORD: cGFzc3dvcmQ=  # base64, NOT encrypted by default
commonMistakes: Assuming a Secret is encrypted just because it's called 'Secret' -- by default it's only base64-encoded, which anyone with cluster read access can trivially decode; real protection needs.
lessons.careerRelevance: Correctly separating config/secrets from container images is expected practice in any real deployment pipeline.
lessons.explain: A ConfigMap holds non-sensitive configuration (URLs, feature flags, config files) as key-value data that can be injected into pods as environment variables or mounted files -- keeping config separate from the container image so the same image works across environments.

lessons.title: Namespaces: organizing a cluster
objectives: Use namespaces to isolate resources within a shared cluster
Explain how namespace changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect namespace with namespace-scoped resources and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A namespace is a way to divide a single cluster into multiple virtual clusters -- useful for separating environments (dev/staging/prod) or teams sharing one physical cluster. Most resources are namespace-scoped (a Service in namespace A can't be found by name alone from namespace B), while some cluster-wide resources (like nodes) are not namespaced at all.
examples:
kubectl get pods -n staging
kubectl create namespace staging
# a Service 'my-app' in namespace 'staging' is reached at:
# my-app.staging.svc.cluster.local from elsewhere in the cluster
commonMistakes: Forgetting to specify -n <namespace> and assuming kubectl commands operate cluster-wide -- most commands default to the 'default' namespace, silently missing resources that live elsewhere.
lessons.careerRelevance: Namespace-based organization is standard practice in any real multi-team or multi-environment cluster.
lessons.explain: A namespace is a way to divide a single cluster into multiple virtual clusters -- useful for separating environments (dev/staging/prod) or teams sharing one physical cluster. lessons.title: Ingress: routing external traffic
objectives: Explain how Ingress routes external HTTP(S) traffic to services
Explain how Ingress changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Ingress with Ingress Controller and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A LoadBalancer Service works, but provisioning one per application gets expensive and doesn't handle path/host-based routing well.
examples:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata: {name: my-ingress}
spec:
  rules:
  - host: myapp.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service: {name: my-app-service, port: {number: 80}}
commonMistakes: Provisioning a separate LoadBalancer Service for every single application -- this is expensive and doesn't scale; Ingress lets many applications share one entry point with routing rules.
lessons.careerRelevance: Ingress is the standard way real-world Kubernetes clusters expose HTTP services to the internet.
lessons.explain: A LoadBalancer Service works, but provisioning one per application gets expensive and doesn't handle path/host-based routing well.

lessons.title: Scaling & the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
objectives: Explain manual and automatic scaling of pod replicas
Explain how horizontal scaling changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect horizontal scaling with Horizontal Pod Autoscaler and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Scaling a Deployment manually (kubectl scale) is simple but requires you to notice load changes yourself.
examples:
kubectl scale deployment my-app --replicas=5

# or, automatically:
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: {kind: Deployment, name: my-app}
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource: {name: cpu, target: {type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 70}}
commonMistakes: Setting no maxReplicas ceiling on an HPA -- an unexpected traffic spike (or a bug causing runaway load) could then scale far beyond what your cluster's actual capacity or budget can handle.
lessons.careerRelevance: Autoscaling is a standard, expected capability in any production Kubernetes deployment handling variable traffic.

lessons.title: Helm: package manager for Kubernetes
objectives: Explain what problem Helm solves over raw YAML manifests
Explain how Helm changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Helm with chart and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A real application often needs many coordinated YAML files (Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, Ingress..) that must be templated per-environment (different replica counts, URLs, resource limits in dev vs prod).
examples:
helm install my-app ./my-app-chart --set replicaCount=3
helm upgrade my-app ./my-app-chart --set image.tag=2.0
helm rollback my-app 1   # back to revision 1 if the upgrade broke something
commonMistakes: Manually copy-pasting and hand-editing YAML files across environments instead of using a templated chart -- this is exactly the repetitive, error-prone process Helm exists to replace.
lessons.careerRelevance: Helm is extremely widely used in real Kubernetes deployments; charts exist for nearly every common piece of infrastructure software.

lessons.title: Rolling updates, rollbacks & troubleshooting a cluster
objectives: Diagnose common pod failure states and safely roll back a bad deployment
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: probe failures.
Explain how CrashLoopBackOff changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect CrashLoopBackOff with ImagePullBackOff and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: When a rollout goes wrong, kubectl rollout undo instantly reverts a Deployment to its previous working revision.
examples:
kubectl rollout status deployment/my-app
kubectl rollout undo deployment/my-app   # revert to the previous revision
kubectl describe pod my-app-x1y2z        # check Events section for the real cause
kubectl logs my-app-x1y2z --previous     # logs from the crashed instance
commonMistakes: Panicking and deleting/recreating resources when a rollout fails, instead of first running kubectl rollout undo -- a safe, instant, well-tested revert path that exists for exactly this.
lessons.careerRelevance: Diagnosing these exact failure states is a routine, practical, daily skill for anyone operating a real Kubernetes cluster. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

quiz.q: What problem does Kubernetes solve beyond what Docker provides?
options: it replaces Docker's container format
orchestrating many containers across many machines: scheduling, healing, and scaling automatically
it makes containers start faster
it removes the need for images

quiz.q: What does 'desired state' mean in Kubernetes?
options: a config file that's never checked again
a declared target (like 'run 3 replicas') that the cluster continuously works to maintain
a synonym for a pod's current status
the initial state before deployment only

quiz.q: What is self-healing in Kubernetes?
options: a feature that fixes bugs in your code
the cluster automatically replacing failed or deleted pods to match the desired state
a manual process an operator must trigger
a synonym for autoscaling

quiz.q: What is the control plane?
options: the machines running your application containers
the set of components (API server, scheduler, etcd) that manage the cluster's overall state
a synonym for a single node
a type of Service

quiz.q: What does the Kubernetes API server do?
options: stores application logs only
acts as the central point every client (kubectl, controllers) talks to in order to read/change cluster state
runs application containers directly
only handles authentication

quiz.q: What does the scheduler do?
options: runs containers directly
decides which node a new pod should run on
stores cluster state
handles external HTTP routing

quiz.q: What is the correct way to interact with a Kubernetes cluster?
options: SSH directly into nodes to manage containers
through the API server, typically via kubectl or another client
editing etcd directly
there is no defined way

quiz.q: What is a pod?
options: a synonym for a container
the smallest deployable unit, which can hold one or more tightly-coupled containers
a type of node
a synonym for a Deployment

quiz.q: Why might a pod hold more than one container?
options: it's never allowed to
for tightly-coupled containers that must share network/storage, like a sidecar shipping logs
to save on Kubernetes licensing costs
pods can only ever hold exactly one container

quiz.q: What does `kubectl get pods` do?
options: deletes all pods
lists pods and their basic status
edits a pod's configuration
shows only a single pod's logs

quiz.q: What does `kubectl describe` show that `kubectl get` doesn't?
options: nothing different
detailed info including recent Events, often revealing the real cause of a problem
only the pod's IP address
the cluster's total node count

quiz.q: What does a Deployment manage?
options: a single, un-replaceable pod
a ReplicaSet, ensuring a specified number of identical pod replicas stay running
only Services, not pods
cluster-wide networking

quiz.q: What happens to a pod managed by a Deployment if it crashes?
options: nothing, it stays crashed until manually restarted
the Deployment automatically creates a replacement to restore the desired replica count
the whole Deployment is deleted
the crash is silently ignored

quiz.q: What is a rolling update?
options: replacing all pods with new ones simultaneously, causing downtime
gradually replacing old pods with new ones, avoiding an all-at-once cutover
a synonym for a rollback
only available in single-replica Deployments

quiz.q: Why do pods need a Service rather than being addressed directly by IP?
options: pods never get IP addresses
pod IPs change constantly as pods are replaced; a Service provides a stable address that always routes to healthy pods
Services are required by Kubernetes licensing
direct pod IPs are faster

quiz.q: What is the default Service type?
options: LoadBalancer
ClusterIP, only reachable inside the cluster
NodePort
Ingress

quiz.q: What does a LoadBalancer Service typically provision?
options: nothing external
an external cloud load balancer routing traffic into the cluster
only internal DNS entries
a ConfigMap

quiz.q: What does a ConfigMap hold?
options: sensitive passwords only
non-sensitive configuration data, kept separate from the container image
container images
cluster node information

quiz.q: Is data in a Kubernetes Secret encrypted by default?
options: yes, always fully encrypted
no, only base64-encoded by default, which anyone with read access can decode
Secrets can't store any data
only if the cluster has zero nodes

quiz.q: What is a namespace used for?
options: speeding up the cluster
dividing a single cluster into virtual clusters, useful for separating environments or teams
a synonym for a node
storing container images

quiz.q: What happens if you forget to specify a namespace in a kubectl command?
options: it operates across the whole cluster automatically
it defaults to the 'default' namespace, potentially missing resources elsewhere
the command fails immediately
it operates on all namespaces simultaneously

quiz.q: Why does Ingress exist, given LoadBalancer Services already work?
options: Ingress replaces the need for Services entirely
provisioning a separate LoadBalancer per app is expensive; Ingress lets many apps share one entry point with routing rules
Ingress is required for any cluster to function
Ingress only works for internal traffic

quiz.q: What does an Ingress Controller do?
options: nothing, Ingress works without one
actually implements the routing rules defined by Ingress resources
replaces the API server
stores cluster secrets

quiz.q: What does the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) do?
options: scales the cluster's node count only
automatically adjusts a Deployment's replica count based on a watched metric like CPU utilization
manually requires an operator to type kubectl scale each time
only works with a fixed number of replicas

quiz.q: Why set a maxReplicas ceiling on an HPA?
options: it's not necessary
without it, a traffic spike or bug could scale far beyond what the cluster's capacity or budget can handle
maxReplicas is required syntax with no real effect
HPA ignores maxReplicas anyway

quiz.q: What problem does Helm solve?
options: it replaces kubectl entirely
packaging many coordinated, templated YAML files as one versioned, installable/upgradable unit
it removes the need for a control plane
it only works for single-container apps

quiz.q: What does `helm rollback` do?
options: deletes the application entirely
reverts an installed chart to a previous revision
installs a brand new chart
only works before the first install

quiz.q: What does `kubectl rollout undo` do?
options: permanently deletes the Deployment
instantly reverts a Deployment to its previous working revision
only works for Services, not Deployments
requires manually rewriting the YAML file first

quiz.q: What does CrashLoopBackOff typically indicate?
options: the pod is running perfectly
the container keeps starting and immediately crashing
the cluster has run out of nodes
the image was never found

quiz.q: What does ImagePullBackOff typically indicate?
options: the container crashed after starting
the specified image doesn't exist or credentials to pull it are missing
the pod is using too much CPU
a networking misconfiguration in the Service

capstone.title: Deploy a full containerized app to Kubernetes with autoscaling and safe rollouts
capstone.description: Take a multi-container application (e.g. a frontend, backend API, and database) and deploy it to Kubernetes end to end: Deployments for each component, Services connecting them, ConfigMaps/Secrets for configuration, an Ingress exposing it externally, and an HPA so it scales under load. Then deliberately roll out a broken version and practice using kubectl rollout undo to recover -- this project should demonstrate the full lifecycle, not just the initial deploy.
deliverables: Deployment + Service manifests for each component of the app
ConfigMap and Secret separating configuration from the container images
An Ingress exposing the app with at least one routing rule
A working HorizontalPodAutoscaler with a documented min/max range and target metric
A written incident note: what you broke on purpose, how you detected it, and the exact rollback command that fixed it
capstone.portfolioTips: Include the full set of YAML manifests in the repo alongside a README with an architecture diagram (even a simple one) and the incident note -- reviewers respond well to evidence you've actually operated something, not just deployed it once.

industryUsage.usage: Kubernetes was originally created at Google, based on internal experience running containers at massive scale with an earlier system called Borg.
Runs its backend microservices architecture on Kubernetes, managing autoscaling and deployment across a large number of independent services.
Migrated its infrastructure to Kubernetes to standardize deployment, scaling, and service discovery across hundreds of internal services.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the difference between a Deployment and a bare Pod?
interviewPreparation.a: A bare Pod, if it crashes or is deleted, is simply gone -- nothing recreates it. A Deployment manages a ReplicaSet that continuously ensures a specified number of pod replicas exist, automatically replacing any that fail, and also manages safe rolling updates when you change the image version.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you debug a pod stuck in CrashLoopBackOff?
interviewPreparation.a: Start with kubectl describe pod to check the Events section for the real cause, then kubectl logs --previous to see the crashed container's actual output. Common causes include a misconfigured command, a missing environment variable/config the app expects, or the app failing its own startup health check.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the difference between a ConfigMap and a Secret?
interviewPreparation.a: Both externalize configuration from the container image, but a Secret is intended for sensitive data. By default a Secret is only base64-encoded, not encrypted -- real protection requires enabling encryption at rest or using an external secrets manager, which is a common point of confusion.

interviewPreparation.q: Why would you use Ingress instead of just a LoadBalancer Service for every app?
interviewPreparation.a: A LoadBalancer Service typically provisions a real external cloud load balancer per Service, which gets expensive and doesn't support host/path-based routing well. Ingress lets many applications share a single entry point (and often a single LoadBalancer) with routing rules based on hostname and path.

interviewPreparation.q: How does the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler decide when to scale?
interviewPreparation.a: It continuously watches a specified metric (commonly CPU utilization) against a target value, and adjusts the replica count up or down within a configured min/max range to keep the metric near that target -- growing under load and shrinking back down as load drops.

interviewPreparation.q: What would you do if a deployment you just rolled out started causing errors in production?
interviewPreparation.a: Run kubectl rollout undo immediately to revert to the last known-good revision -- it's fast, safe, and doesn't require improvising a manual fix under pressure. Investigate the actual root cause afterward, with the system already stable again.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the practical benefit of using Helm instead of raw kubectl apply with YAML files?
interviewPreparation.a: A real application often needs many coordinated, environment-specific YAML files. Helm packages these as one templated, versioned chart, so installing, upgrading, and rolling back the entire application is a single command instead of manually tracking and editing many separate files.

description: Orchestrating containers at scale -- pods, Deployments, Services, Ingress, ConfigMaps, Secrets, Helm, and autoscaling.
